strengths: The paper studies an important problem: removing hand-crafted behavioral descriptors from quality-diversity reinforcement learning.
Representing policies through kernel mean embeddings of occupancy measures is intuitive and provides a principled connection between policy behavior, MMD, and random Fourier features.
The method integrates with an established QD optimizer and is evaluated on six continuous-control environments against several conceptually distinct baselines.
AutoQD obtains strong empirical results, especially on ground-truth QD score, and the dynamics-variation experiment provides a practically meaningful test of repertoire utility.

The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and includes useful implementation details and ablations. weaknesses: The central theoretical result appears incorrect. The proof derives |a²-b²|=|a-b|(a+b)≤4|a-b| and then uses this upper bound to infer a tail bound on |a-b| from a bound on |a²-b²|. That implication goes in the wrong direction without a positive lower bound on a+b. Consequently, Theorem 1 does not establish the stated MMD-distance guarantee.

The theory analyzes embeddings constructed from i.i.d. occupancy-measure samples, whereas the implemented embedding uses correlated transitions from finitely truncated trajectories. Equation 6 does not have exactly the same expectation as the infinite-horizon occupancy embedding unless truncation is explicitly corrected or negligible. No corresponding finite-trajectory guarantee is given.

The cited uniform random-feature convergence bound is stated without assumptions such as a bounded state-action domain or the associated radius/bandwidth dependence. Several MuJoCo observation spaces are not formally bounded, further weakening applicability of the theorem.

The iterative descriptor-update procedure is underspecified. The initialization of the affine descriptor before the first scheduled PCA update is absent, and Algorithm 1 does not say whether archived policies are re-embedded and reassigned to cells when the descriptor map changes. Keeping old cell assignments would make the archive inconsistent with the current descriptor.

The evaluation is not fully fair across method classes: QD methods may return thousands of policies, whereas SMERL and DvD-ES are configured with only 10. Vendi score, oracle best-policy adaptation, and archive-summed ground-truth QD score all benefit from larger candidate populations. Equal-size subsampling or population-size curves are needed.

The ostensibly method-agnostic Vendi evaluation uses the same occupancy-RFF representation that motivates AutoQD. Using independent random features avoids direct reuse but does not remove the representational alignment; complementary diversity metrics based on trajectories, learned evaluators, or task outcomes are needed.

Only three training seeds are reported, with no paired tests or confidence intervals beyond standard errors. Several results have substantial uncertainty, and all ablations are restricted to one environment with three seeds.

Some claims about dimensionality reduction are overstated: PCA projection does not generally preserve the embedding geometry, and subsequent axis-wise calibration further changes distances. PCA variance also need not correspond to behaviorally important variation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: objective offsets and evaluation embedding dimensionality are not specified, the qVS normalization description does not by itself guarantee individual scores in [0,1], and the DvD-ES implementation citation contains a placeholder “(link).” Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the invalid central theorem and unresolved evaluation and algorithmic ambiguities place the submission below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of quality-diversity methods: their dependence on manually designed behavioral descriptors.
Representing policy behavior through occupancy-measure kernel mean embeddings is intuitive, computationally simple, and compatible with existing QD algorithms.
The manuscript is generally well organized and evaluates six continuous-control environments against several conceptually relevant baselines.
The reported final-performance gains are large in several domains, and the appendix provides useful implementation parameters and limited dimensionality ablations.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is not established. The theorem and proof repeatedly confuse the embedding norm, its square, MMD, and MMD squared. Most critically, Eq. 34-36 proves |a^2-b^2| <= 4|a-b| but then uses this inequality in the reverse direction to derive the claimed concentration bound for |a-b|. Earlier concentration steps similarly switch between squared and unsquared quantities. The stated theorem therefore does not follow from the proof.

The practical embedding in Eq. 6 is not covered by the theorem, which assumes i.i.d. occupancy-measure samples. Transitions within a trajectory are dependent, and the finite truncated discounted sum does not have exactly the claimed occupancy-measure expectation without accounting for truncation. Thus, even a repaired theorem would not directly justify the implemented method.

The empirical comparison is substantially confounded by unequal population sizes. QD methods can return archives containing thousands of policies, whereas DvD-ES and SMERL are configured with only ten policies. GT QD score, Vendi score, and the best-policy-under-perturbation evaluation all directly benefit from having a much larger candidate population, so these results do not isolate representation quality.

The Vendi metrics use essentially the same RFF occupancy representation that motivates and is optimized by AutoQD. Using independent random features does not eliminate this representational alignment, making the supposedly method-agnostic evaluation partly circular. No complementary trajectory-, state-, action-, or task-level diversity metrics are presented.

The adaptation experiment selects the best archive member separately for each altered environment, requiring oracle evaluation of the entire population after the dynamics are known. Larger archives receive a severe multiple-comparisons advantage, and the reported uncertainty over evaluation episodes does not measure variation across independently trained populations.

Only three training seeds are used, with no hypothesis tests or confidence intervals beyond standard errors. This is particularly inadequate for stochastic evolutionary optimization and for conclusions based on several environments and metrics.

Essential ablations are missing: ordinary versus fitness-weighted PCA, fixed versus periodically updated descriptors, occupancy embeddings versus simpler trajectory statistics, state-only versus state-action features, alternative kernels or bandwidths, and equal-sized/equal-budget population comparisons. The provided dimensionality ablations cannot establish which proposed components cause the gains.

The algorithm is underspecified when descriptors change. Algorithm 1 updates the affine descriptor map but does not rebuild the archive, relocate existing policies, or reconcile cell thresholds computed under previous descriptor maps. Updating observation-normalization statistics also changes the effective kernel and may make stored embeddings mutually inconsistent. These omissions affect both correctness and reproducibility.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no released code or precise accounting of environment interactions across methods, some baseline modifications are substantial, handcrafted descriptors are not fully formalized, and the DvD-ES implementation is referenced only by a placeholder '(link)'.

The methodological novelty is limited: the main construction combines standard random Fourier kernel mean embeddings, PCA, and an existing CMA-MAE optimizer. Given the invalid central proof and confounded evidence, the paper does not currently substantiate a top-tier contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of quality-diversity reinforcement learning: dependence on manually designed behavioral descriptors.
Representing policies through kernel mean embeddings of occupancy measures is intuitive, broadly applicable, and integrates cleanly with existing QD algorithms.
The empirical scope is reasonably strong: six continuous-control environments, five diverse baselines, multiple quality/diversity metrics, a dynamics-shift study, and dimensionality ablations.
AutoQD achieves substantial gains in ground-truth QD score across all six environments and strong Vendi-based results in most environments, suggesting genuine practical promise.
The manuscript is generally clear and provides useful implementation details, computational costs, and pseudocode.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not established by the supplied proof. Equations 34–36 show that the squared-distance error is upper-bounded by four times the distance error; this cannot be used to derive the claimed upper-tail bound on the distance error in Equation 37. Near zero, converting squared-distance error to distance error requires a square-root-type bound or an assumption that the sum of the distances is bounded away from zero.

Other theoretical steps also require stronger justification. Hoeffding's inequality is applied directly to a nonlinear squared norm of dependent pairwise terms, and the cited uniform random-feature approximation appears to omit bounded-domain or diameter assumptions. Continuous-control state spaces need not satisfy the unstated compactness conditions.

The theory analyzes embeddings formed from i.i.d. occupancy-measure samples, whereas the implemented embedding uses correlated transitions from finite trajectories. Its expectation equals the desired infinite-horizon embedding only absent truncation error, and no concentration result is given for this practical estimator. Updating observation-normalization statistics may additionally change the feature map over time, but the handling of previously stored embeddings is unspecified.

Evaluation uses only three training seeds, with no statistical tests or confidence intervals beyond standard errors. Several reported differences have high variance, and the dynamics-shift AUC table provides no uncertainty across training runs.

The comparison across paradigms is potentially confounded by population size and interaction budget. SMERL and DvD-ES produce only ten skills/policies, while QD methods can return much larger archives; both Vendi Score and ground-truth QD score can benefit directly from larger collections. Environment-step budgets are not normalized or clearly reported.

The supposedly method-agnostic VS/qVS evaluation uses occupancy-based random Fourier embeddings closely aligned with AutoQD's own representation. Independent random features do not remove this shared inductive bias, so additional trajectory-, state-, or action-based diversity measures are needed.

Ablations are limited to dimensionalities on one environment. The paper does not isolate the effects of fitness weighting, calibration, PCA, descriptor-update scheduling, kernel bandwidth, state normalization, or occupancy embeddings relative to simpler state-visitation alternatives.

Descriptor updates are operationally under-specified: the paper does not clearly explain whether and how all archive members are re-embedded and reinserted when the PCA map changes. Without rebuilding the archive, its existing cell assignments would correspond to obsolete descriptors.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the DvD-ES implementation citation contains a literal '(link)' placeholder, no code release is identified, and important details about rollout horizons, out-of-bound descriptors, evaluation population selection, and total environment interactions are missing.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of quality-diversity optimization: dependence on domain-specific behavioral descriptors. The proposed combination of occupancy-measure embeddings, random Fourier features, dimensionality reduction, and CMA-MAE is intuitive, modular, and computationally practical.

The empirical study covers six continuous-control environments and compares against several meaningfully different approaches, including handcrafted QD, learned-descriptor QD, evolutionary diversity, and unsupervised RL baselines.

AutoQD obtains strong ground-truth QD scores across the tested tasks. The additional descriptor-dimension, embedding-dimension, weighting, rollout-count, stability, adaptation, and qualitative analyses provide useful evidence beyond a single headline table.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with extensive pseudocode, architecture and hyperparameter information, limitations, and qualitative descriptions of the discovered behaviors.
weaknesses: The proof of the central MMD approximation theorem is invalid as written. Equations 34–36 establish |a²−b²|≤4|a−b|, but Equation 37 then incorrectly uses a concentration bound on |a²−b²| to obtain the claimed bound on |a−b|. The implication goes in the wrong direction; near zero, one generally obtains a square-root dependence instead. Thus the stated finite-sample theorem, a central claimed contribution, is unsupported.

The theoretical assumptions are insufficiently specified. Uniform random-feature approximation over all state-action vectors generally requires a bounded domain or related regularity assumptions, yet the theorem is stated for arbitrary occupancy measures and is applied to continuous-control spaces. The claimed one-to-one correspondence between policies and occupancy measures also only holds modulo policy choices at states with zero occupancy, rather than literally for every policy.

The evaluation uses only three training seeds for nearly all main comparisons and provides no uncertainty-aware significance analysis. Several reported standard errors are large, making conclusions based on ranks or isolated means fragile.

Some evaluation metrics favor the proposed representation or large repertoires. Vendi Score uses essentially the same RFF occupancy representation that motivates AutoQD, albeit with separate features, while ground-truth coverage and counts of successful policies are sensitive to population size. Comparing archives containing potentially thousands of policies against methods configured with only ten skills or policies therefore does not cleanly isolate behavioral diversity.

The adaptation experiment performs oracle selection of the best policy separately for each altered environment and counts successful members of differently sized populations. This demonstrates that a repertoire contains useful policies, but does not establish an implementable adaptation procedure and can substantially advantage larger archives.

Important implementation details are ambiguous: when the descriptor map changes, the paper does not clearly state whether every archived policy is re-embedded and the archive is rebuilt; similarly, evolving observation-normalization statistics could make stored embeddings inconsistent unless they are recomputed. These details affect both correctness and reproducibility.

The ablations do not adequately attribute the gains to the main design choices. Stronger controls should include fixed versus iteratively updated projections, unweighted PCA across all tasks, random projections, simpler state/trajectory statistics, and sensitivity to kernel bandwidth. The weighting ablation on one environment finds no significant benefit, while the low-dimensional projection itself has no guarantee of preserving the MMD geometry.

AutoQD's diversity sometimes comes with substantially reduced policy quality, particularly in HalfCheetah and BipedalWalker, and it does not consistently win the quality-weighted diversity metric. This makes the broad claim of discovering both diverse and high-performing policies less conclusive than the ground-truth QD-score results alone suggest.

strengths: The occupancy-measure perspective provides an intuitive, domain-agnostic basis for representing policy behavior, and random Fourier features make the resulting representation computationally practical.
AutoQD is clearly described and combines its learned representation with an established QD optimizer through a relatively simple affine descriptor map.

The empirical study covers six continuous-control environments and includes handcrafted-QD, learned-descriptor, evolutionary, and RL baselines, as well as adaptation experiments and several ablations.
The paper reports complementary quality and diversity metrics and provides useful qualitative examples and candid discussion of failure modes in HalfCheetah and Walker2d.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is not established as written. Equations 34–37 use |a²-b²|=|a-b|(a+b)≤4|a-b| to infer a tail bound on |a-b| from a bound on |a²-b²|; this inequality has the wrong direction for that inference. At best, the available relation yields a square-root dependence. Equation 14 also appears to omit the finite-sample scaling discrepancy in the cross term.

The invoked uniform random-feature approximation suppresses assumptions and constants related to a bounded input domain and its diameter. The theorem is stated for general state-action vectors, while several evaluated environments have effectively unbounded observation coordinates, so the claimed bound does not directly apply.

The practical embeddings can differ substantially from the analyzed occupancy embeddings. With γ=0.999 and trajectories of roughly 1000 steps, the stated truncation term γ^T is about 0.37 rather than negligible; early termination makes it policy dependent. Thus the empirical representation is not convincingly connected to the advertised occupancy-measure geometry.

The main cross-family evaluation is strongly confounded by population size. AutoQD and other archive methods may return thousands of policies, whereas DvD-ES and SMERL use only 10. Vendi Score is bounded by population size, and GT-QD score, successful-policy counts, and oracle best-policy adaptation all improve simply from evaluating more candidates. The claim that Vendi Score enables fair comparison across differently sized populations is therefore misleading. Equal-size subsampling and compute/sample-matched comparisons are needed.

The adaptation experiment selects the best policy after evaluating the entire population under each altered dynamic. This is oracle selection rather than an operational adaptation procedure and gives large archives a major multiple-opportunity advantage.

The representation and archive update mechanics are underspecified. Algorithm 1 changes the descriptor map but does not explicitly rebuild the archive under the new coordinates; retaining incumbents assigned with older descriptors would make cell comparisons inconsistent. Likewise, continually updated state-normalization statistics can invalidate previously stored embeddings unless trajectories or embeddings are recomputed, which is not explained.

Only three seeds are used for the main results despite large standard errors, with no statistical tests or confidence analysis for the principal comparisons. The sole eight-seed PCA-weighting ablation finds no significant effect, weakening the justification for a named component of the method.

The evaluation diversity kernel closely mirrors AutoQD's own occupancy/RFF representation. Using separate random features avoids literal reuse but not metric alignment, so the strong Vendi results are partly method-favoring; more independent behavioral measures and equal-population comparisons are necessary.

The conceptual novelty is moderate: kernel mean embeddings, random Fourier features, PCA, and CMA-MAE are established components, while the new combination is not supported by a correct theorem or sufficiently controlled evaluation to justify the paper's stronger claims.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and meaningful approach to automatically constructing behavior descriptors by combining occupancy-measure kernel mean embeddings, random Fourier features, calibrated weighted PCA, and CMA-MAE.
The occupancy-measure perspective provides a principled definition of behavioral similarity and is better motivated than proxy descriptors based only on reconstruction or terminal states.

The empirical study is broad for this area: six continuous-control environments, five relevant baselines, multiple complementary quality/diversity metrics, an adaptation experiment, qualitative examples, and several ablations.

AutoQD achieves strong results overall, including the best ground-truth QD score in all six tasks and generally strong Vendi and quality-weighted Vendi scores. The dynamics-shift experiment provides a useful downstream demonstration of why diverse repertoires matter.

The paper is clearly written and unusually forthcoming about failure modes in HalfCheetah and Walker2d. The appendices provide substantial implementation details and analyses of descriptor dimensionality, embedding dimensionality, rollout count, and descriptor stability.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 1 contains an invalid final implication. Equations 34–36 establish |a²-b²| ≤ 4|a-b|, which does not allow a concentration bound on |a²-b²| to imply the stated bound on |a-b|. A valid generic implication gives |a-b| ≤ sqrt(|a²-b²|), resulting in a different error and tail-rate dependence. Thus, the theorem as stated is not proved, although a weaker convergence result appears repairable.

The empirical evidence relies on only three seeds for the main comparisons, despite several large standard errors. No statistical tests or confidence intervals for pairwise main-result differences are supplied, making some claims of superiority uncertain.

Evaluation fairness is imperfect. Vendi-based metrics use essentially the same occupancy/RFF notion of diversity that motivates AutoQD, while ground-truth QD score and adaptation counts favor methods returning large archives. SMERL and DvD-ES return only ten policies, and the paper does not establish matched environment-interaction or computational budgets across algorithm families.

Important method-level ablations are absent: occupancy RFF embeddings versus simpler state/action statistics, unweighted or fixed PCA across all tasks, fixed versus periodically updated descriptors, and sensitivity to kernel bandwidth, discount factor, and update schedule. The current ablations are mostly restricted to BipedalWalker.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete. In particular, the manuscript does not fully specify how continually updated observation normalization interacts with previously stored embeddings, how archives are remapped when descriptors change, and all preprocessing used for evaluation embeddings. The promised source-code link is also blank in the submitted PDF.

The claimed one-to-one correspondence between policies and occupancy measures needs qualification: policies can differ on zero-occupancy states while inducing the same occupancy measure, and the statement depends on the policy class and observability assumptions. This does not invalidate the method but overstates its theoretical motivation.

The novelty is primarily in a well-executed composition of established tools—kernel mean embeddings/RFFs, PCA, and CMA-MAE—rather than a fundamentally new learning principle. Given the proof issue and evaluation confounds, the evidence supports a marginal accept rather than a confident accept.
